output:
Peter, I appreciate the payroll experience behind your view. You’re right that an informal, recurring advance can leave people permanently short, create difficult leaver balances, and turn HR into a lender. I’d be wary of keeping the current arrangement as it is. But I’d be cautious about assuming that closing it makes the underlying need go away.

We tried that in 2025. We closed our scheme in February after Finance raised much the same concerns. We gave two months’ notice and ran a financial-literacy session with our SACCO. In the six months that followed, reception logged 61 calls from debt collectors and loan apps. Some callers were contacting supervisors listed as “referees.” That is not a complete measure of staff borrowing, and I can’t say every call was caused by the closure. But it was a striking change from the handful we had seen before, and it gave us evidence that at least some of the need had moved outside the workplace rather than disappeared.

We also saw more unplanned absence on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. Again, that’s an operational observation, not proof that the policy change caused each absence. Still, it made us ask whether the costs of closure were simply landing in other departments, where they were harder to see in a Finance forecast.

So in September we reopened advances under written rules—not the old informal arrangement. Staff submit requests through the payroll portal, not to HR’s office. The limit is 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, repaid in full at the next payroll, with no fee. We check the proposed deduction against the Employment Act’s limit that total deductions must not exceed two-thirds of wages. The aim is to avoid someone being left with nothing at month-end; the 40% cap is a separate, more conservative policy limit, not the legal threshold.

Since reopening, we’ve had roughly 55–70 requests a month, averaging about KES 9,000. We’ve recovered everything except balances from two leavers, with total write-offs of about KES 14,000 for the year. Those figures don’t prove the scheme is right for every workplace, and the requests do mean some real payroll and administrative work. But they give Finance a defined volume, repayment date and ceiling to plan around. Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme because the forecast impact is known in advance; it is a fixed limit, not a surprise.

I also agree that financial literacy is useful, and that a SACCO should be part of the conversation. But it may not be a workable answer for every short-notice emergency. SACCO loans can take two to three weeks and require guarantors. That doesn’t help much when a child has been sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. For someone on KES 28,000 a month, a small, affordable emergency advance may be a different proposition from taking several high-cost app loans while waiting for another option.

One case has stayed with me: a loader at our Changamwe depot had taken loans from six apps by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to pay another. It took four months of work with payroll to unwind the situation. I don’t offer that as proof that a company advance prevents app borrowing. It does, however, make me question whether “they’ll adjust” is safe to assume for everyone—or whether an unstructured gap can become more expensive for both the employee and the business.

For your meeting on the 18th, Brenda, I’d put the comparison on paper rather than argue from a feeling. Include the direct costs of administering advances and the amount that might be written off, but also ask what you can measure about absence, missed shifts or runs, supervisor time, and collection calls to the workplace. Keep those categories distinct: the calls and operational disruption matter, but they are not automatically costs caused by the advance policy. If you can, compare a trial period with a clear policy against the recent baseline, and review it after a few months.

A possible policy to discuss with Finance could include:

- A fixed maximum per pay cycle, expressed as a percentage of net pay.
- No more than one advance per cycle.
- Full repayment through the next payroll, with no fee.
- Requests and approvals through a documented route—such as the payroll portal—with clear roles for HR and Finance.
- A check that the deduction fits within the legal limit and leaves the employee with a reasonable amount of take-home pay.
- A review date, with Finance tracking outstanding balances, repayments, leavers and forecast impact.

Your Finance Manager is right to be concerned about cash flow and repeated advances. Peter is right that payroll needs clear controls and that recovery from leavers can be difficult. I’d take those concerns seriously, but I wouldn’t treat a clean shutdown as evidence that staff no longer need short-term money. In our case, a tightly bounded policy turned an informal, hard-to-forecast practice into something Finance could see and plan for. That may not be the answer for your firm, but it seems worth testing against the alternative before deciding.
